extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys and litigants (including pro se) litigating unauthorized disclosure claims under 26 U.S.C. §§ 6103 and 7431
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and litigation of civil claims for unauthorized disclosure of tax returns and return information under 26 U.S.C. § 7431 and related provisions of § 6103, including defenses under § 7431(b) and procedural prerequisites such as notice/assessment rules under §§ 6212/6213.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory cause of action under 26 U.S.C. § 7431(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If any officer or employee of the United States knowingly, or by reason of negligence, discloses any return or return information with respect to a taxpayer in violation of any provision of section 6103, such taxpayer may bring a civil action for damages against the United States in a district court..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To state a claim the plaintiff must show (1) disclosure of 'return' or 'return information'; and (2) that the disclosure was in violation of §6103; and (3) that the disclosure was made knowingly or by reason of negligence. The petition emphasizes that §7431(a) makes disclosure wrongful if 'knowingly or negligently' made and that a plaintiff need only plead the elements of the statutory claim (Hrubec v. Amtrak).

rubrics_metrics.name: §7431(b) good-faith-erroneous-interpretation defense
rubrics_metrics.description: "No liability shall arise under this section with respect to any disclosure which results from a good faith, but erroneous, interpretation of section 6103."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow, statutory defense limited to disclosures that actually result from a good-faith but erroneous interpretation of §6103; it is not a general 'good faith' defense. The defendant bears the logical burden of introducing and proving reliance on §6103 as the basis for disclosure; courts should not require the plaintiff to plead 'bad faith' to avoid early dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages formula under §7431(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: On finding liability the defendant shall be liable for (1) the greater of $1,000 for each act of unauthorized disclosure or actual damages plus, in willful or grossly negligent cases, punitive damages; and (2) the costs of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages analysis includes per-act statutory minimum ($1,000 each) versus actual damages; punitive damages available for willful/grossly negligent disclosures; attorneys' fees/costs recoverable. Number of discrete disclosures can affect total statutory recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations under §7431(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An action ... may be brought ... at any time within 2 years after the date of discovery by the plaintiff of the unauthorized disclosure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and discovery questions are critical — disputes often arise about when the plaintiff discovered the disclosure (e.g., publication dates of notices). Courts may treat some disclosures as time-barred depending on when discovery occurred and whether earlier disclosures were considered. Appellate opinions may differ on which disclosures were timely considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: General confidentiality requirement of §6103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Returns and return information shall be confidential, and except as authorized by this title ... shall not disclose return or return information obtained by him in any manner in connection with his service as such an officer or an employee ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A threshold inquiry in §7431 litigation is whether the information disclosed was 'returns' or 'return information' within §6103 and thus confidential. If information is not confidential under §6103, §7431 liability does not arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'return information' under §6103(b)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The term 'return information' means (A) a taxpayer's identity, the nature, source, or amount of his income, payments, receipts, deductions, credits, assets, liabilities, net worth, tax liabilities, tax withheld, deficiencies ... or other data ... and (B) any part of any written determination or any background file document ... which is not open to public inspection ... but such term does not include data in a form which cannot be associated with, or otherwise identify, directly or indirectly, a particular taxpayer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether particular material falls within this statutory definition determines confidentiality. De-identified data that cannot be associated with a taxpayer is excluded. The statute also preserves the Secretary's discretion to withhold selection standards if disclosure would impair enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limitation of §6103(k)(6) disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: "An internal revenue officer or employee may ... disclose return information to the extent such disclosure is necessary in obtaining information ... with respect to the correct determination of tax, liability for tax, or the amount to be collected or with respect to the enforcement of any other provision of this title. Such disclosures shall be made only in such situations and under such conditions as the Secretary may prescribe by regulation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §6103(k)(6) authorizes limited investigative disclosures 'to the extent necessary' to obtain information. Courts construe 'necessary' narrowly — it authorizes disclosures to obtain information, not broadly to publicize while collecting an invalid assessment. Regulations (26 C.F.R. §301.6103(k)(6)-1) describe permitted investigative contexts (examination, collection, enforcement) and emphasize necessity/conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two judicial tests for §7431 liability: 'confidentiality test' vs 'validity test'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some circuits apply a 'confidentiality test' (once information is in public domain, it loses §6103 protection), while others apply a 'validity test' (return information remains confidential unless there is authority to make the disclosure at the time it is made — procedural validity matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This circuit split affects whether liability can attach when earlier disclosures occurred or when the underlying assessment was invalid. Under the confidentiality test, prior public disclosure can bar damages; under the validity test, an invalid assessment or lack of statutory/administrative authority at the time of disclosure can make subsequent disclosures unauthorized even if similar information had been publicly released earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural validity of assessments and effect on disclosure authorization (§6212/§6213/§6203)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions drawn from §§ 6212, 6213, and §6203: a notice of deficiency must be mailed to the taxpayer's 'last known address' to be valid; §6213 restricts assessment/collection until notice is mailed and relevant periods expire; §6203 concerns the recording of an assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a notice of deficiency was not properly mailed to the taxpayer's last known address, the assessment and resulting lien may be invalid; disclosures made to collect or publicize an assessment that is invalid may be unauthorized under §6103. Courts differ on whether the procedural invalidity of an assessment negates §6103(k)(6) authorization — central to the 'validity test.' Certified mailing lists and postal forms often constitute prima facie evidence of proper mailing absent contrary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption/evidence of proper mailing of notices of deficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A postal form certifying that a notice of deficiency has been mailed is sufficient, in the absence of contrary evidence, to establish that the notice was properly mailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate cases (e.g., Zolla, Williams, Cool Fuel) recognize certified mailing records and Form 3624 as adequate proof of mailing; defendants frequently rely on such evidence to show assessments were validly commenced. Plaintiffs must introduce contrary evidence to rebut the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading burden regarding 'bad faith' and allocation of proof on §7431(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff need not plead that disclosures were made in 'bad faith.' Section 7431(b) creates an affirmative defense; defendants must introduce and prove that the disclosure resulted from a 'good faith, but erroneous, interpretation of §6103.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not shift the burden onto plaintiffs to plead bad faith to preserve claims; defendants are the logical parties to introduce evidence of a §6103-based interpretation. Where defendants do not properly plead or present the §7431(b) defense, courts should not require plaintiffs to negate it prior to discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for evaluating 'good faith' under §7431(b) (Harlow analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good faith defense under §7431(b) should be judged by an objective standard analogous to that in Harlow v. Fitzgerald: whether the contours of the statutory right were sufficiently clear that a reasonable official would understand that the action violated the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the unlawfulness was 'apparent' in light of preexisting law; the defense is not defeated only because the precise action was not previously held unlawful. Circuit precedent on what constitutes 'clearly established' law guides the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'necessary' in §6103(k)(6) — obtaining information vs collecting
rubrics_metrics.description: §6103(k)(6) authorizes disclosures 'to the extent such disclosure is necessary in obtaining information ... with respect to the correct determination of tax, liability for tax, or the amount to be collected ...' and 'does not permit disclosures while actually collecting the assessment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe §6103(k)(6) as limited to disclosures needed to obtain information; disclosures that are part of collection efforts to publicize or enforce an invalid assessment exceed this authorization. This distinction is central in disputes where an assessment's validity is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit conflict significance — need for higher court resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a recognized conflict among circuits about whether prior public disclosure defeats §7431 liability (confidentiality test) or whether procedural validity of the assessment at the time controls (validity test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where circuits are split (Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, Tenth, etc., favoring validity test; Ninth and some others favoring confidentiality test), litigants may seek certiorari to resolve the tension. Appellate briefing should marshal precedent distinguishing the tests and argue which approach correctly respects statutory text and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial treatment of combined procedural/timing issues (rehearing, judgment entry, certiorari timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing rules for appellate relief and certiorari: petitions for rehearing may toll the period for certiorari; whether a revised opinion or withdrawn opinion constitutes a new 'judgment' for timing purposes affects certiorari deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking Supreme Court review, parties must carefully analyze whether an appellate court's withdrawal and replacement of an opinion altered the 'judgment' for certiorari timing; rehearing filings under Fed. R. App. P. 40(a) and case law (Missouri v. Jenkins, FCC v. League of Women Voters, FTC v. Minneapolis-Honeywell) govern tolling. This is procedural law relevant to appellate practice rather than substantive §7431 liability but is treated in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Secretary's discretion to withhold certain disclosures under §6103(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the statute requires disclosure of standards used for selection of returns for examination, or data used for determining such standards, if the Secretary determines that such disclosure will seriously impair assessment, collection, or enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where some return information might appear related to selection or enforcement, the Secretary may lawfully withhold certain categories of internal data if disclosure would impair tax administration; litigants should consider this statutory protection when arguing whether particular material must be disclosed.
